items.prompt: How is a peregrine falcon able to reach such extreme speed when diving onto prey?

options.label: It beats its wings unusually fast throughout the dive
options.feedback: During the dive itself the wings are folded and barely move at all; the speed comes from something other than flapping harder.

options.label: Rising warm air carries it downward at speed
options.feedback: Warm rising air lifts a soaring bird upward, the opposite direction to a dive, so it cannot be what drives this kind of plunge.

options.label: It folds into a narrow shape and lets gravity do the work
options.feedback: Tucking its wings tight against its body and diving almost straight down turns the falcon into a narrow, streamlined shape that gravity accelerates with very little air resistance to slow it.

options.label: It pushes off from a higher perch than other birds use
options.feedback: Height of the starting perch affects how long a dive can build speed for, but the shape the falcon holds during the fall is what lets that speed reach such extremes in the first place.

items.ok_line: A narrow, folded shape lets gravity do almost all the work.
items.ko_line: Think about the falcon's shape during the dive, not about flapping or where it started.
items.exp_title: A narrow shape falling under gravity
items.exp_text: Rather than flapping to build speed, a diving peregrine falcon folds its wings tightly against its body and drops in a steep, controlled plunge, letting gravity itself do almost all the accelerating. Shaped this way, the falcon presents very little surface for air to push back against, so it keeps speeding up for much of the dive instead of levelling off the way an open-winged bird would; falcons have been clocked diving at speeds no other animal on Earth reaches in level flight. Small adjustments to its tail and the angle of its folded wings let it steer that narrow, plunging shape precisely enough to strike a moving target at the very bottom of the dive.

items.prompt: What lets a cheetah reach such extreme speed across open ground?

options.label: A very flexible spine lengthens every stride
options.feedback: Its spine flexes and extends dramatically with each bound, letting the front and back legs reach much further apart than a stiffer-backed animal's stride ever could, adding significant length to every single stride.

options.label: Extra-large lungs let it breathe far more air
options.feedback: Lung size helps sustain effort over a longer run, but the raw top speed itself comes mainly from how far each stride reaches, not from how much air is moving through the lungs.

options.label: Retractable claws grip the ground like cleats
options.feedback: Cheetah claws are unusual for a cat because they stay out permanently rather than pulling back in, and that fixed, ever-ready grip is closer to what actually helps its speed.

options.label: It carries very little weight in its legs
options.feedback: Light legs help a cheetah accelerate and change direction quickly, but the extreme top speed itself comes chiefly from stride length rather than leg weight alone.

items.ok_line: A spine that bends and stretches, adding reach to every single stride.
items.ko_line: Think about the cheetah's back arching and stretching with every bound.
items.exp_title: A spine that adds length to every stride
items.exp_text: A cheetah's backbone flexes far more than that of most other animals, curling tight through one part of each stride and stretching long through another, and that extra flex lets the front and back legs land much further apart than a stiffer spine would ever allow. Combined with claws that stay permanently exposed for a firm grip on the ground, and a long, muscular tail used to counterbalance sudden turns, a cheetah has been recorded running faster over open ground than any other land animal alive. That extreme pace cannot be held for long, because the effort generates heat inside the body faster than a cheetah can get rid of it.

items.prompt: How does a sailfish reach such extreme bursts of speed in the water?

options.label: It leaps out of the water to avoid drag
options.feedback: A sailfish's fastest bursts happen while it stays submerged and swimming, not while it is airborne clear of the water.

options.label: It swims in the wake of larger fish for a free push
options.feedback: The burst of speed described here comes from the sailfish's own body and fins, not from riding behind another animal.

options.label: Its rough skin reduces friction with the water
options.feedback: Skin texture plays some small role in many fast swimmers, but the sailfish's dramatic top-speed bursts come chiefly from changes in its body shape rather than its skin.

options.label: It folds its large fins flat to cut drag while sprinting
options.feedback: Normally raised for steering, display, or herding schools of smaller fish, its tall dorsal fin and other fins press down flat against the body during a sprint, letting the sailfish slip through the water with far less resistance.

items.ok_line: Fins folded flat trade their usual job for a burst of pure speed.
items.ko_line: Think about the sailfish's tall dorsal fin, and what happens to it during a sprint.
items.exp_title: Folding away what usually slows it down
items.exp_text: Much of the time, a sailfish keeps its tall, sail-like dorsal fin raised, using it to help herd schools of smaller fish and to signal to other sailfish nearby. When it needs to sprint, though, it presses that fin and its other large fins down flat against its body, trading the drag they normally cause for a smoother, narrower shape; sailfish have been recorded reaching some of the highest sustained speeds measured in any fish this way. Raising the fins again immediately after the burst brings back their everyday uses, at the cost of the extra speed the flattened shape allowed for a moment.

items.prompt: Why does a tiger beetle often stop abruptly in short bursts while chasing prey across open ground, rather than sprinting the whole way in one smooth run?

options.label: It is checking the air for scent of its prey
options.feedback: Scent plays little part in this particular chase; the stopping pattern is linked to a different sense entirely.

options.label: It runs too fast for its eyes to keep the target in view
options.feedback: Relative to its own tiny body length its running speed is extraordinary, and at that pace its eyes cannot gather and process enough light quickly enough to keep the moving prey in clear view, so it must stop briefly to relocate its target before dashing forward again.

options.label: It is resting its legs after each short dash
options.feedback: The pauses are far too brief and happen far too early in the chase to be about tired muscles; something to do with its senses is forcing the stop, not fatigue.

options.label: It is avoiding the shadows of passing birds overhead
options.feedback: These brief stops happen during a chase on open ground regardless of anything overhead, and they are tied to keeping track of the prey it is chasing rather than to any danger from above.

items.ok_line: Running so fast its own eyes lose the target, and having to stop to find it again.
items.ko_line: Think about what its eyes actually need in order to form a clear image while it runs.
items.exp_title: Running faster than its own eyes can track
items.exp_text: Scaled up to the size of its own body, a tiger beetle's sprint is among the fastest running performances measured in any animal, but that speed comes at a cost. Its eyes need a certain amount of time to gather enough light and process a clear image, and at full sprint the beetle is covering ground faster than its eyes can keep up, so the image of its prey effectively blurs into the background. Stopping briefly lets its eyes catch up and relocate the target precisely, after which it dashes forward again in another short, sightless burst.

items.prompt: How can a Greenland shark end up living for centuries longer than almost any other animal with a backbone?

options.label: It stops ageing completely once fully grown
options.feedback: This shark's body still ages gradually throughout its life; what differs is how slowly that ageing proceeds, not a complete stop to the process.

options.label: It hibernates for most of each year
options.feedback: This shark stays active and swimming year-round rather than entering any dormant, sleep-like state for extended stretches.

options.label: Its whole body runs at an extremely slow pace in cold water
options.feedback: Living in near-freezing deep water, its metabolism runs at an unusually slow rate, its growth crawls forward at only a small pace each year, and that same slow pace of living appears to stretch out its entire lifespan far beyond that of animals whose bodies run faster.

options.label: It replaces its whole body with new cells regularly
options.feedback: There is no evidence this shark replaces its body this way; its extended lifespan is linked to how slowly its body operates overall, not to any process of full renewal.

items.ok_line: A whole body running in slow motion, and a life stretched out to match.
items.ko_line: Think about the cold, near-freezing water this shark lives in, and what that might do to its whole metabolism.
items.exp_title: A life lived in slow motion
items.exp_text: Deep, near-freezing water keeps a Greenland shark's whole metabolism running at a fraction of the pace common in warmer-water animals, and every process in its body, including growth, unfolds correspondingly slowly. Scientists have estimated the age of individual sharks using proteins in the lens of the eye, which change at a known, steady rate over an animal's life, and some Greenland sharks have turned out to be older than any other vertebrate known. A body that runs this slowly seems to accumulate the ordinary wear of living at a correspondingly gentle pace, stretching out a lifespan far beyond what a faster-living animal's body could sustain.

items.prompt: Why can a giant tortoise live so much longer than most other animals of similar size?

options.label: Its body grows and ages at an unusually slow pace
options.feedback: A giant tortoise grows slowly across its whole life, and its cells appear to accumulate damage at a correspondingly gentle rate, a pattern strongly linked in many animals to living an especially long life.

options.label: Its thick shell protects its organs from all injury
options.feedback: A shell defends well against predators and rough handling, but it cannot slow down the internal ageing process happening inside the tortoise's own cells.

options.label: It hibernates through most of its life
options.feedback: A giant tortoise stays active through most of the year in its natural range and does not spend the bulk of its long life in any dormant state.

options.label: It stops eating once fully grown to conserve energy
options.feedback: A tortoise continues to feed regularly throughout its adult life; going without food is not part of what extends its lifespan.

items.ok_line: Slow growth and slow wear, matched to a slow whole life.
items.ko_line: Think about the pace of everything this animal does, from growing to moving.
items.exp_text: Many slow-growing, cold-blooded animals age at a pace roughly matched to how slowly the rest of their body operates, and a giant tortoise is an extreme example of that pattern. Its cells divide and its tissues wear down only gradually across its life, and giant tortoises in captivity have been recorded living for well over a century and a half. That same unhurried pace of living, evident in everything from its slow growth to its slow movement, appears to be closely tied to how long its body manages to keep functioning.

items.prompt: How can a bowhead whale live for centuries while carrying far more cells, and so far more chances for something to go wrong, than a small short-lived animal?

options.label: Its enormous size alone slows down ageing directly
options.feedback: Among mammals, larger size is loosely linked with longer life on average, but size alone does not explain how this particular whale so dramatically outlives other large animals; something more specific is at work in its cells.

options.label: It replaces its skeleton completely every few decades
options.feedback: A whale's skeleton is not periodically replaced wholesale; bone tissue is maintained and repaired gradually rather than rebuilt from scratch.

options.label: It carries almost no cancer-causing mutations to begin with
options.feedback: With so many cells living for so long, this whale should by simple odds accumulate plenty of harmful mutations over its lifetime; what differs is thought to be how effectively its body deals with the damage, not an absence of it in the first place.

options.label: Genes that repair damaged DNA work unusually well
options.feedback: Studies of the bowhead whale's genes have found unusually effective versions of genes involved in repairing damaged DNA and suppressing cells that turn cancerous, which may let its enormous number of cells keep functioning correctly far longer than in most other mammals.

items.ok_line: Genes tuned to repair damage more effectively, not just a body that happens to be big.
items.ko_line: Think about what has to happen inside a cell to stop small errors from turning into serious damage.
items.exp_title: Cells that repair themselves unusually well
items.exp_text: Every cell in a whale's enormous body accumulates small errors in its DNA over time, and with vastly more cells living for vastly more years than in a small animal, a bowhead whale should by simple odds face a correspondingly higher risk of that damage causing serious harm. Genetic studies of bowhead whales have identified versions of certain genes, involved in repairing DNA and in stopping damaged cells from multiplying out of control, that appear to work especially effectively in this species, and bowhead whales are thought to live well past two centuries. That level of internal repair, rather than anything about its sheer size alone, seems to be what lets so many cells keep working correctly across a lifespan stretched out so far.

items.prompt: How can a mantis shrimp's small claw strike hard enough to crack open a shell in a fraction of an instant?

options.label: Its muscles alone contract with extreme force
options.feedback: Muscle alone, contracting directly, could not release energy fast enough to explain a strike this sudden; something is storing that force ahead of time and releasing it all at once.

options.label: A saddle-shaped spring stores energy before releasing it in an instant
options.feedback: Muscles slowly load energy into a curved, spring-like structure in the claw over a longer stretch of time, and a latch then holds that tension until it releases all at once, snapping the claw forward far faster than a muscle contracting directly could ever manage.

options.label: It builds up an electric charge and delivers a shock
options.feedback: No electrical charge is involved in this strike at all; the force comes from a purely mechanical spring-and-latch arrangement inside the claw.

options.label: It swings its whole body to add momentum to the claw
options.feedback: The strike is delivered almost entirely by the claw itself snapping forward; the rest of the body barely needs to move for the strike to land with full force.

items.ok_line: A spring loaded slowly, then let go all at once.
items.ko_line: Think about something inside the claw being loaded up slowly, well before the strike itself happens.
items.exp_title: A latch holding back a loaded spring
items.exp_text: Deep inside a mantis shrimp's claw sits a curved, saddle-shaped structure that stores elastic energy, much like any bent material under tension, as muscles slowly load it up well before the strike itself begins. A latch mechanism holds all that stored energy in place until it releases in an instant, snapping the claw forward so fast that the water in front of it briefly boils from the pressure change, faster than any muscle contracting on its own could ever manage. The strike lands with such sudden force that it can crack open the armoured shells of snails and crabs that would otherwise resist a much slower blow entirely.

items.prompt: Why does a sloth move so much more slowly than almost any other mammal its size?

options.label: Its muscles are unusually weak and cannot move faster
options.feedback: A sloth's muscles work well enough for their purpose; the slowness is closer to a deliberate strategy matched to its situation than a simple case of physical weakness.

options.label: It is simply too heavy to move any faster
options.feedback: A sloth is a fairly light, small-bodied mammal for its size; weight is not what is limiting how fast it can move.

options.label: Its diet supplies barely enough energy to move quickly
options.feedback: Leaves are extremely low in the kind of energy an animal can quickly draw on, and a sloth's whole body, including how it moves, appears built to spend as little energy as possible to match what that meagre diet can actually supply.

options.label: It stays still mainly to hide from predators
options.feedback: Staying motionless does help a sloth go unnoticed, but this animal actually moves this slowly even when it has no predator anywhere nearby, which points to something deeper than simply avoiding notice.

items.ok_line: A body spending only as much energy as its thin diet can actually supply.
items.ko_line: Think about what a sloth eats, and how much usable energy that food could possibly provide.
items.exp_title: Moving only as fast as its fuel allows
items.exp_text: A leaf-heavy diet delivers only a small, slow trickle of usable energy compared with the food eaten by most other mammals of similar size, and a sloth's whole body seems built around living within that limited budget. Its metabolism runs at a notably reduced pace, its muscles work in slow, deliberate movements rather than quick bursts, and a sloth can spend an entire day barely covering the ground a similarly sized mammal might cross in only a few minutes. Moving that slowly costs very little energy, which matches almost perfectly with how little energy its stomach is able to supply it with each day.

items.prompt: Why can a termite queen live for decades while worker termites from the very same colony live only a fraction as long?

options.label: Her body is protected from ageing in ways workers' bodies are not
options.feedback: Despite carrying the very same genes as her workers, a queen's body appears to suppress the processes that cause ordinary ageing far more effectively, and she is fed, groomed and sheltered in ways that spare her the daily wear a worker's body endures.

options.label: She stops working entirely and so never wears her body out
options.feedback: A queen's body still works constantly at laying eggs, an intense, ongoing physical demand; her long life is not explained by simply resting or being inactive.

options.label: Workers are simply born from a different, shorter-lived species
options.feedback: A queen and her workers all hatch from the very same population and carry essentially the same genetic material; the huge difference in how long they live comes from something else entirely.

options.label: She is replaced by a new queen every few years without anyone noticing
options.feedback: A single termite queen is generally the same individual leading the colony continuously for a very long stretch, rather than being secretly and repeatedly swapped out.

items.ok_line: Same genes, same colony, but a body switched to age very differently.
items.ko_line: Think about what makes a queen's body different from a worker's, given that both hatch from the same population.
items.exp_title: Two very different lifespans from the same genes
items.exp_text: A termite queen and the workers all around her hatch from essentially the same genetic starting point, yet a worker typically lives only a season or two while a queen can go on for decades, an enormous gap for animals this closely related. Which role an individual grows into is decided early on and appears to switch on very different patterns of gene activity, patterns that seem to protect a queen's cells from the kind of damage that builds up in a worker's body through constant daily labour. Even sharing the very same colony and the very same genetic starting point, the two castes end up ageing at almost entirely different speeds.
